props.title: Infection
props.initialSlug: Hospital horror turns staff into infectious killers

sections.content: Infection (2004) stands as a pivotal entry in Japanese medical horror, following the psychological breakdown of staff at a decrepit hospital during one hellish night. Director Masayuki Ochiai crafts a fever dream that shares DNA with earlier J-horror classics like Cure (1997) and Pulse (2001), but adds distinctly medical anxieties. The film's sickly green color palette and decaying hospital setting influenced later medical horror like The Autopsy of Jane Doe (2016) and The Taking of Deborah Logan (2014).

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a golden age for Japanese horror cinema, with Infection emerging alongside powerhouses like Ju-On: The Grudge (2002) and Dark Water (2002). These films shared a focus on institutional breakdown - hospitals, schools, apartment buildings - as sites of supernatural terror. Infection's emphasis on contamination and institutional failure feels especially prescient today, predating outbreak films like Contagion (2011) and The Flu (2013).

The film's signature "green death" concept influenced body horror techniques in later works like The Green Inferno (2013) and Contracted (2013). Its exploration of medical malpractice and cover-ups connects to a broader Japanese horror tradition of institutional critique seen in films like Suicide Club (2001) and Premonition (2004). sections.content: Infection helped establish key tropes of modern medical horror: isolated hospital settings, spreading contagion, and moral corruption among medical staff. These elements appear refined in later works like The Void (2016) and Re-Animator (1985). The film's emphasis on guilt and collective responsibility echoes through contemporary Japanese horror like Tag (2015) and Creepy (2016).
